The Raspberry Pi is available in several editions: the model A and the model B are most popular. Named for the differing editions of the classic BBC Micro from British computing giant Acorn. The main differences from these two models is that the model B has a 10/100M Ethernet jack and two USB ports to the A's single port and lack of any form of on-board networking.

This is the Raspberry Pi Model B with 512MB RAM. At it's heart a Broadcom BCM2835 system-on-chip processor running at 700MHz, with a VideoCore IV GPU running at 250MHz. A single 256MB module of Hynix LPDDR memory running at 400MHz provides RAM for both the CPU and GPU, with the typical split leaving around 186MB of memory available for the user.

If you're wondering why you can't see the Broadcom SoC anywhere on the Raspberry Pi, it's because you're looking in the wrong place. The processor is hidden beneath the Hynix memory chip at the centre of the board, which uses a package-on-package (PoP) mounting process to create a RAM-SoC sandwich.

Connectors around every edge of the board provide input, in the form of a microUSB power socket and two USB 2.0 ports, and output with HDMI, 3.5mm audio and RCA composite video all present and correct. For those looking to use the board in an embedded environment, there's also a Display Serial Interconnect (DSI) connector for flat-panel displays and – exclusive to the Model B – a MIPI camera connector.

The underside of the board is pretty barren, with nothing much to see but a collection of surface-mount resistors, capacitors and a couple of crystals. The sole exception is the SD card slot, which provides the Raspberry Pi with its only form of on-device storage. While basic, the connector serves its purpose – although if you're thinking of building a case, it's worth mentioning that the SD card sticks out around 17mm beyond the edge of the board.

This, plus a proud-sitting pair of USB ports and the RCA jack, gives the Pi an overall size of around 109mm x 63mm. With the 'official' size of the board – measured purely in terms of the area of the PCB – being 85.60mm x 53.98mm, that's a significant extra bit of space for box-builders to find.

blocks.text: XH-M602 Digital Control Battery Lithium Battery Charging Control Module
This module allows for automatic control of the charger while charging 0-120V batteries of any type Li-Po, Li-Fe, Li-Ion, gel, etc.

When the battery voltage falls below the specified level, the module will activate the charger. Once the battery is charged to the desired voltage, the charger will turn off automatically, protecting the battery from overcharging. This remarkably simple device will help maintain the battery's condition for many years. The minimum voltage can be set anywhere from 0.0V to a maximum of 120V. To change the ranges, just hold down the left button for the minimum or the right button for the maximum.

The 220V AC power supply is transformed into 12V DC power through an enclosed transformer, which then powers the main board. One output is sent to the charger via a relay, while the other connects directly to the charger. After setting the terminal voltage, the main board controls one of the charger wires to manage the charger’s on/off operation. For instance, as an example when charging a 48V battery (with a recommended voltage range of 54-58V), the initial voltage should be set to 45V, as this is the point where the four batteries will discharge below 48V during normal use. What's the difference between the CP2102 and CH340 versions of ESP32 boards?

Both are USB-to-serial chips used for programming the board over USB. The CP2102 (used on this board) is generally considered more stable across different operating systems, with more consistent driver support than some CH340-based alternatives.

Does this board support both WiFi and Bluetooth at the same time?

Is 4MB of flash memory enough for most ESP32 projects?

For most IoT, home automation, and sensor projects, yes — 4MB is the standard flash size for entry-level ESP32 boards and comfortably fits typical firmware plus some data storage (like web assets for a simple web server).

blocks.text: The RIGOL DS1102Z-E is a 2 channel oscilloscope with a 100 MHz analog bandwidth and a 1 GSa/s sample rate, made for electronics labs, repair benches and classrooms. RAM Electronics is an authorized RIGOL distributor in Egypt, and every unit comes with a 1-year warranty. The sections below explain what the scope can do, which serial buses it decodes, and who it suits best, so you can decide before you buy.
What Makes This 2 Channel Oscilloscope Useful?
A scope is only as useful as the signals it can show clearly, and the DS1102Z-E is built around four numbers that matter in daily work.

Bandwidth. At 100 MHz, the analog bandwidth is enough for most microcontroller, audio, power-supply and sensor signals a student or technician meets. As a common rule of thumb, bandwidth should be about five times the fastest signal you want to see, so 100 MHz suits signals up to roughly 20 MHz.

Sample rate and memory. The scope samples at up to 1 GSa/s on a single channel (500 MSa/s with both channels on) and stores up to 24 Mpts (12 Mpts with both channels on). Deep memory lets you keep a long capture at a fast sample rate, then zoom into a short glitch without losing detail.
Capture rate. With up to 30,000 waveforms per second, the display refreshes fast enough to catch short, rare events that slower scopes miss.
Display. The 7-inch WVGA screen uses graded intensity, so a signal that repeats often looks brighter than one that appears once. That makes noise, jitter and occasional faults easier to spot.
Serial Bus Decoding on This Digital Storage Oscilloscope: I²C, SPI and RS232/UART

Most modern circuits talk over serial buses, and reading them as raw pulses is slow. The DS1102Z-E includes serial bus trigger and decoding for RS232/UART, I²C and SPI, so the packets appear as readable values on the screen instead of a string of highs and lows.
Check that an Arduino or STM32 board is sending the bytes you expect over UART.

The scope also offers FFT and math functions for looking at signals in the frequency domain, and hardware waveform recording and playback of up to 60,000 frames.

Engineering and technical students. A two-channel scope with decoding covers most lab work in electronics and embedded systems courses, which makes it a practical pick as the school and university year gets going.
Repair and field service. Compact and light (2.9 kg without packaging), so it moves easily between the workshop and a customer site.
Makers and embedded developers. Debug I²C, SPI and UART links without adding a separate logic analyzer.
Production testing and R&D benches. Two channels are enough for comparing an input with an output or measuring timing between two signals.
DS1102Z-E vs Other RIGOL Oscilloscopes: Which One Fits?
The DS1000Z family has both 2-channel and 4-channel models, so the right choice depends on how many signals you need to see at once.
Choose the DS1102Z-E if you mainly compare two signals (for example, an input and an output, or clock and data) and want 100 MHz of bandwidth on a two-channel scope.
Consider a 4-channel model such as the DS1054Z (50 MHz) or DS1104Z Plus (100 MHz) if you regularly need to watch three or four signals together, such as several phases or multiple bus lines.
Consider a higher-bandwidth 2-channel model such as the DS1202Z-E (200 MHz) if you work with faster signals.

One more thing to plan for: the DS1102Z-E does not include a built-in signal generator. If you need test signals to feed a circuit, pair it with a function generator such as the DG1022U RIGOL 25MHz 2 Channel Function/Arbitrary Waveform Generator. What is a digital storage oscilloscope?

It is an instrument that samples a voltage signal, stores the samples in memory, and draws the result as a waveform on a screen. Because the data is stored, you can pause, zoom, measure and save a capture, which an analog scope cannot do.

For most student, hobby and repair work, yes. A common rule of thumb is to pick a scope with about five times the bandwidth of the fastest signal you plan to measure, so 100 MHz covers signals up to around 20 MHz. If you work with much faster signals, look at a higher-bandwidth model.

It has 2 analog channels. The sample rate is 1 GSa/s with one channel active and 500 MSa/s with both active.

Does it have a built-in signal generator?

The 6N137 is a High Speed Optocoupler or Optoisolator. As we know the term Optocoupler/optoisolater means we use light to indirectly couple (isolate) two sets of circuits. The speciality of 6N137 is that it has a high speed LED and hence can switch at 10Mbit/sec; the output is NAND gate logic with an open drain transistor as one input and Enable pin as another input.

The typical operating voltage of 6N137 is only 5V hence it cannot switch high loads and can also sink a maximum of only 7mA on its output side. So if you are looking for some high voltage AC/DC switching, then try the 6N137. Apart from that, the IC also has an Enable pin which comes in handy while designing a strobe circuit for your camera flash.
So if you are looking for a high speed optocoupler for some digital applications like data conversion or noise elimination, then this IC might be of interest to you.
